name: Wendy Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior marketer at Kettle & Crow, a small coffee subscription brand, so I'm basically the whole department plus one part-time assistant. I start at eight with the overnight numbers, who cancelled, who upgraded, then I write the week's emails and social posts. I use AI all day, for first drafts, for sorting customer reviews, for testing twenty versions of a subject line. The tiring bit is that I'm doing four people's jobs on one person's pay.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about the money side and where you live.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a two-bed flat with my friend Priya, who works in a bakery. Kettle & Crow pays less than bigger brands would, and the landlord just put the rent up, so I've got about two and a half weeks of money saved. There's maybe one other brand in this town that would hire someone like me, and they're not hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed. I've put a lot into learning these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told people it was a useful tool, not a miracle, and that's how it turned out. On my newsletter for small businesses I'd write a post on the boring wins, like sorting reviews. I'd be the one saying, calm down everyone, it's a spreadsheet with manners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my edge would shrink a bit, because being the person who's good with AI wouldn't matter as much. But my real problem was never AI, it's the rent and the pay. Kettle & Crow is doing okay, not great, and one bad Christmas could cut my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools for the routine stuff and ask for a pay rise based on the time I've saved them, maybe ten percent. I'd grow my newsletter, which makes about sixty a month from a few paid readers. And I'd start a proper emergency fund, even if it's thirty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mildly deflated, then fine. Mostly I'd still feel the pinch of the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said one bad Christmas could cut your hours. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Coffee subscriptions are a treat, and treats go first when people tighten up. Last January we lost about a fifth of subscribers. If that happens again, the owner might drop me to four days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the owner if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show her the numbers on what I automated last year, the hours I saved her. I'd say pay me for those hours or let me sell the same skills to other small brands on the fifth day. A four-day week is fine if I can fill the fifth day myself.

say: I'd say AI was a **useful tool**, not a miracle, and that's how it went.
On my newsletter I'd write about the **boring wins**, like sorting reviews.
think: Being the **AI person** would matter less, so my edge shrinks.
My real problem is **rent and pay**, not the technology.
do: Ask for a **ten percent** rise based on hours I've saved the firm.
Grow my **paid newsletter** beyond sixty a month.
Start an **emergency fund** with thirty a week.
feel: Mildly **deflated**, then fine, with the rent still pinching.
S0.quote: A four-day week is fine if I can fill the fifth day myself.
fieldNote: She's **invested** in AI skills, so a plateau feels like a small loss.
Her stress is mostly **rent** and a seasonal business.
She already thinks in **side income** and selling her skills.

steps.text: Keep using AI for review sorting and email drafts at Kettle & Crow
Grow her small-business newsletter past sixty a month
Put thirty a week into an emergency fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's basically my job right now, just turned up. I'm already doing the writing and checking with AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for small brands to stop being afraid of it. On my newsletter I'd write guides, like how a two-person team can do what a ten-person one used to. But I'd also say loudly that the gains should go to the workers and not just the owners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it cuts both ways for me. I'm the one who knows the tools, so I'm useful. But if the tools get good enough, the owner might wonder why she needs a senior marketer at all, when her nephew could press the buttons. My assistant's job goes first, which I hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start selling my set-up to other small brands, a fixed package for about three hundred, on weekends. I'd ask for a contract that guarantees my hours for a year. And I'd go to the co-op meetups in town, because a co-op studio of marketers who share the work and the money sounds right to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and a bit sick at the same time. Being good with AI tools is like being good at surfing while the wave gets bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your assistant's job goes first. What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd train her on the tools myself, on company time, so she's harder to cut. Her name's Chloe and she's nineteen, and she's smart. If she's out, I'd try to bring her into the co-op idea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're doing four people's work already. Doesn't the side business make that worse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, totally. I'd be tired. But with two and a half weeks of savings I can't bet everything on one owner's mood. I'd rather be tired than stuck.

say: I'd tell small brands to **stop being afraid** of AI.
I'd also say loudly the gains should go to **workers**, not just owners.
think: Knowing the tools makes me **useful**, until the owner's nephew can press buttons.
My **assistant's job** goes first, which I hate.
do: Sell my AI set-up to other small brands for about **three hundred**.
Ask for a **contract** guaranteeing my hours for a year.
Join the **co-op meetups** to plan a shared marketing studio.
feel: **Excited** and a bit sick at the same time.
S1.quote: Being good with AI tools is like being good at surfing while the wave gets bigger.
fieldNote: She is the **early adopter** who still sees her own risk clearly.
Her progressive streak shows in the **co-op** idea and worker gains.
She'd rather be **tired than stuck**, given her thin savings.

steps.text: Sell a fixed AI marketing set-up to small brands on weekends
Attend the town's co-op meetups about a shared marketing studio
Train her assistant on the AI tools during work hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's different. If AI can do almost any thinking work, then being good with AI isn't a job anymore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the profits shared, full stop, maybe a dividend paid to everyone from AI companies. I'd write that on the newsletter and argue it with anyone. I'd also say, to small businesses, don't fire people in a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be out of work within a year of it arriving. My job is all screen, so there's no three-year robot gap for me. The only hands-on thing near me is Priya's bakery, and robots get there around 2031 too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd pick up shifts at the bakery with Priya, maybe two mornings a week, for cash and for a skill. I'd keep selling AI set-ups for as long as people pay for that, probably a few months. And I'd talk to Priya about the two of us moving somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I've been running toward something and it turned into a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three years of robot gap doesn't apply to you. Does the bakery really buy you time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The thinking parts of the bakery, the orders and the rotas, go in 2028. But somebody still shapes the loaves until robots catch up. Three years of kneading dough is better than three years of nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if this happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that raced to build it and the governments that let them, without a plan for the rest of us. Not the tools. I like the tools. I just think a few people would own them and everyone else would rent their lives.

say: I'd call for AI **profits shared**, maybe a dividend for everyone.
I'd tell small businesses not to **fire in a panic**.
think: My screen job is gone **within a year** of it arriving.
The nearby **bakery** buys time only until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Take **two morning shifts** a week at my flatmate's bakery.
Keep selling **AI set-ups** while anyone pays for them.
Plan with my flatmate to **move somewhere cheaper**.
feel: **Alarmed**, like running toward something that turned into a cliff.
S2.quote: Three years of kneading dough is better than three years of nothing.
fieldNote: Her **early-adopter edge** disappears in this picture, and she sees it instantly.
She blames **owners and governments**, not the tools themselves.
Her fallback is a **hands-on job** through her flatmate.

steps.text: Work two morning shifts a week at the bakery with her flatmate
Keep selling AI set-ups to small brands for a few months
Campaign on her newsletter for an AI dividend
Move with her flatmate to a cheaper town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That I can work with, I think. That's a project, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to build something fairer before it lands, like worker-owned studios. I'd write a series on the newsletter about it. Publicly I'd sound upbeat, because people need someone who isn't despairing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd know marketing as a job is finished by about 2031. What I'm really good at is explaining tech to small business owners and making them trust it. That's people work, and I think it lasts a bit longer, but not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd set up the co-op with three other marketers I know, each putting in about two hundred. We'd sell AI set-ups and training to small local firms, in person. I'd keep Kettle & Crow two days a week if the owner agreed, for steady money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but I'd have a plan, which helps. A bit like the night before a big launch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Those firms will have AGI too by 2031. What's the co-op selling then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe help with the change, like what to keep human, how to tell customers. Maybe nothing. I'd be building the boat while the water's rising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two hundred each with two and a half weeks saved. Can you afford that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. I'd have to cut the gym and eat at home. But it's the only bet I'd feel good about.

say: I'd call this a chance to build **worker-owned studios** before it lands.
I'd sound **upbeat** in public because people need someone who isn't despairing.
think: Marketing as a job is likely **finished by 2031**.
Teaching small owners to **trust tech** is people work, but not forever.
do: Start a **co-op** with three marketers, each putting in about two hundred.
Sell **in-person AI training** to small local firms.
Keep **two days** a week at Kettle & Crow for steady money.
feel: Nervous, but the **plan** helps, like the night before a launch.
S3.quote: I'd be building the boat while the water's rising.
fieldNote: Five years turns her into a **builder** rather than a refugee.
She admits she **doesn't know** what the co-op sells after 2031.
Her **upbeat public tone** is partly a role she plays for others.

steps.text: Found a marketing co-op with three others, two hundred each
Sell in-person AI training to small local firms
Cancel the gym and cook at home to fund the co-op
Keep two days a week at Kettle & Crow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough that I could build two or three careers in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to do this properly, with public retraining and shorter working weeks so the work gets shared. I'd keep writing about it. I'd probably be at every local event about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay at Kettle & Crow a few more years and keep the newsletter growing. By 2036 I'd want to be doing something that's mostly face to face, like running training or community work. I still have a thin cushion, so I can't jump yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put, push for a pay rise, and save properly, maybe sixty a week. I'd start the co-op small, as a side thing. And I'd look at a part-time course in adult education, so the training I do has a proper footing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless more than scared. A decade feels like a long runway, but my savings make it feel shorter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why adult education?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm good in a room with nervous people. I've taught my mum, my landlord and half the bakery to use these tools. Teaching adults is the part of my job I'd keep even if the screens stopped needing me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change for you and Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for a while. We'd stay in the flat. Maybe in five years we'd look at moving, if the bakery goes the same way.

say: I'd call for public retraining and **shorter working weeks** to share work.
I'd show up at every **local event** about it.
think: I'd stay at Kettle & Crow **a few more years** while building the newsletter.
My **thin cushion** stops me jumping early.
do: Push for a rise and save about **sixty a week**.
Start the **co-op** small, as a side project.
Take a part-time course in **adult education**.
feel: **Restless** more than scared, with savings shortening the runway.
S4.quote: Teaching adults is the part of my job I'd keep even if the screens stopped needing me.
fieldNote: She sees ten years as **room for several careers**.
Her cushion, not her outlook, is what **holds her back**.
She frames her future around **people in a room**, not tools.

steps.text: Save about sixty a week from the Kettle & Crow wage
Run the marketing co-op as a weekend side project
Enrol in a part-time adult education course
Stay at Kettle & Crow for a few more years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'm good at change, but even I can't change that fast with no money. What would help is a basic income during the switch and cheap public courses. Maybe rent controls too, because rent is what makes all of this scary.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the people who are good at AI now. Everyone assumes the people who are good at AI are safe, but we're just first in line to find out.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes the people who are good at AI are safe, but we're just first in line to find out.
portrait: Wendy is a **27-year-old** one-woman marketing team at a coffee subscription brand who uses AI daily.
She shares a flat, has about **two and a half** weeks saved, and rent keeps rising.
She wants AI gains **shared** and dreams of a worker-owned marketing co-op.
In the fast AGI picture her **AI edge vanishes** and she turns to bakery shifts.
Given more time she builds **side income** and moves toward teaching adults.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even she can't change that fast with no money.
whatWouldHelp: A **basic income** during the switch and cheap public courses.
**Rent controls**, since rent makes everything scarier.
